**Rime** is a daily allocator. Each morning it splits capital between leveraged equity
ETF exposure, a volatility hedge, and cash. It has been running live on Alpaca since
April 2026.

There are three parts to it: a base signal, a macro and risk overlay on top of that, and
the infrastructure that runs the whole thing unattended. I take them in that order below.

```{=html}
<div class="metrics">
<div class="metric"><div class="metric-value">1.86</div><div class="metric-label">Sharpe, simulated</div><div class="metric-note">2012&ndash;2025 &middot; SPY 0.92</div></div>
<div class="metric"><div class="metric-value">1.58</div><div class="metric-label">Sharpe excluding 2020</div><div class="metric-note">the honest number</div></div>
<div class="metric"><div class="metric-value">&minus;17%</div><div class="metric-label">Max drawdown, simulated</div><div class="metric-note">SPY &minus;34% same window</div></div>
<div class="metric"><div class="metric-value">~44%</div><div class="metric-label">Average gross exposure</div><div class="metric-note">not fully invested</div></div>
</div>
```

The gap between those two Sharpe figures is 2020. The volatility hedge had a huge run
during the COVID crash, and a stretch like that lifts the headline number for the entire
period. I publish both because 1.58 is the better guide to what the strategy does in an
ordinary year.

::: {.note-strip}
Figures above are **simulated** results from a historical backtest over 2012–2025,
not live trading results. Simulated performance has inherent limitations: it is
constructed with hindsight, does not reflect the impact of real order flow, and does
not guarantee future results. A live track record is available on request.
:::

## The problem

Leveraged index ETFs decay in choppy markets. They rebalance daily, so the compounded
return depends on the path and not just the endpoint. A sideways market grinds them down
even when the index finishes flat. Holding one indefinitely is a bet that volatility
stays low.

So I asked something narrower: can I hold that exposure only while the drag is small, and
sit somewhere else the rest of the time?

## How it decides

**The base signal.** A shallow decision tree over a set of trend and volatility state
variables. I kept it shallow on purpose. Fourteen years of daily bars is not a big
sample, and every extra split is another chance to fit noise.

**The macro and risk overlay.** The macro layer uses cross-asset series that tend to move
ahead of equities instead of alongside them. On top of that sits a volatility circuit
breaker that cuts leveraged exposure when volatility spikes. It runs on hysteresis, so
the level that switches it on is not the level that switches it off. Without that, the
allocation thrashes around a single threshold. A rebalance deadband covers everything
else: if the target has not moved much, nothing trades.

::: {.note-strip}
I do not publish the specific state variables, macro series, or thresholds here.
Happy to walk through them in an interview.
:::

## The infrastructure

**One decision function.** Research and production call the same function. There is no
separate notebook that approximates the live system. That gap is how a backtested
strategy quietly stops being the strategy you tested.

**State that survives a crash.** State persists between runs in a JSON-backed store
written atomically, so an interrupted run resumes cleanly instead of rebuilding its view
of the current regime from a truncated window. Order handling is idempotent, so a retry
after a partial failure does not double-submit.

**Data quality gates.** Market and macro feeds come through a pipeline with Parquet
caching, data-quality checks, and lookahead-safe time alignment. Bad ticks, stale bars,
and missing sessions get caught before anything reaches the allocator. If the feed looks
wrong, the system sits out.

**47 pytest tests** across the decision tree, state transitions, gating logic, and the
risk overlays. They cover regime transitions, breaker behavior at the hysteresis
boundaries, and deadband logic. Mostly they exist so I can change things without
guessing.

**Monitoring.** A Streamlit and Plotly dashboard surfaces live positions, system state,
and performance. Anything running unattended needs to be legible when it looks wrong.

## Validation

One backtest number does not tell you much, so I put it through a few things that could
have killed it:

```{=html}
<table class="spec">
<tr><th>Walk-forward folds</th><td>Parameters fit on one window, evaluated on the next, rolling forward. No single global fit.</td></tr>
<tr><th>Pre/post-2020 splits</th><td>2020 is an outlier regime that flatters almost any volatility-responsive strategy. Reported separately for exactly that reason.</td></tr>
<tr><th>Slippage &amp; commission stress</th><td>Costs scaled well past realistic levels to find where the edge disappears.</td></tr>
<tr><th>Block bootstrap</th><td>Resampling in blocks to preserve autocorrelation, testing whether results depend on the specific historical path.</td></tr>
</table>
```

Of those four, the 2020 split is the one that changed how I report the strategy. Quoting
only the number that includes 2020 would overstate what Rime does in a normal year. That
is why both figures are at the top of this page instead of buried down here.

## What I'd do next

- Swap the shallow tree for a probabilistic regime model, and check honestly whether it beats the rules instead of assuming it will.
- Model execution against intraday liquidity instead of assuming a fill at the daily close.
- Widen the macro overlay carefully. More inputs means more degrees of freedom.
